title: AI security best practices: A practical guide for IT teams and MSPs
summary: AI security best practices start with seeing where AI is already in use. Learn seven repeatable steps to manage AI risk across your environment.
body_markdown:
AI security best practices give all IT organizations a clear playbook for using AI tools safely, without slowing down the people who rely on them. Adoption is moving faster than most teams can track, and employees reaching for new tools are usually trying to work faster, not cause harm.


This guide walks you through seven practical steps you can put into action today, starting with finding where AI already runs in your environment. You’ll learn what belongs in an acceptable use policy, how to protect sensitive data at the point of use, where least privilege applies to AI tools and agents, and how to keep the evidence auditors and insurers increasingly expect.


## **Why AI security best practices matter now**


AI security best practices matter now because adoption is outpacing visibility, and many teams lack a clear view of which AI tools are in use across their environments, who is using them, and what data those tools can access. Employees may use public chatbots to draft reports, paste source code into AI assistants to debug faster, or run browser extensions that connect to AI services. They aren’t necessarily acting maliciously. They’re trying to work more efficiently, often with tools that IT hasn’t inventoried or approved.


That gap creates real exposure. Shadow AI, the unsanctioned use of AI tools across an environment, is where most AI security risks hide. A[Gartner survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-19-gartner-identifies-critical-genai-blind-spots-that-cios-must-urgently-address0) of 302 cybersecurity leaders, conducted March to May 2025, found that 69% of organizations suspect or have evidence that employees are using prohibited public generative AI. Sensitive data processed by an external AI service may create compliance exposure under requirements such as HIPAA, PCI DSS, and GDPR, depending on the data and circumstances. Auditors and cyber insurers have started asking organizations for AI inventories, yet those without sufficient visibility can struggle to produce them. The AI security guidelines below help turn that blind spot into something teams can identify, assess, and govern.


## **Seven AI security best practices for IT teams and MSPs**


The seven AI security best practices below follow a logical sequence: see what’s running, set rules, protect data, control access, vet vendors, monitor and record, then plan for incidents and train people. Each step builds on the one before it, and together they form a loop you can run again every time a new tool appears. You don’t need to tackle all seven at once, but the order matters, because you can’t govern what you can’t see.


### **See which AI tools are already in use**


Start by building visibility into every AI tool running across your environment. Shadow AI spreads through browsers, extensions, IDE plugins, command-line tools, and plain API access, often with nothing installed locally. Traditional software inventory misses most of it. A list that includes ChatGPT alongside every other installed app won’t tell you who used it, when, or what data they submitted.


Real visibility goes beyond installed software to include browser extensions and IDE plugins, detect DNS traffic to AI services that endpoint-only tools can miss, attribute usage to specific users and devices, and classify tools by vendor and approval status.[N-able Shadow AI Visibility](https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-able-shadow-ai-visibility-is-now-available-to-help-govern-ai-usage-n-central-n-sight-and-adlumin) , available in N-central, N-sight, and Adlumin, detects AI apps, browser extensions, and network access using existing technology, helping teams produce an AI inventory on demand. Visibility provides the foundation for effective policy and control.


### **Set a clear AI acceptable use policy**


Write a short, plain-language AI acceptable use policy that names which tools are approved and what data can go into them. A policy you can’t tie to real usage is unenforceable, which is why visibility comes first. Keep it readable. People follow rules they understand, and a dense legal document that nobody reads protects no one.


At a minimum, cover approved and prohibited tools, the data types that must never go into a public model, who owns enforcement, and how someone requests approval for a new tool. For deeper policy design, including risk tiers, ownership models, and documentation requirements, lean on established AI governance standards rather than building from scratch.


### **Protect sensitive data in prompts**


Keep sensitive data out of prompts, because client records, source code, and credentials can leave an organization through a chat box that traditional data-loss tools never see. Data loss prevention was built for files, attachments, and destinations, not for text typed into a browser. A paste into an AI tool slips past that older stack entirely, and after the fact, no one can say what was shared or with which model.


The only reliable point to catch this is the interaction itself, as it happens. Inspection at the point of use can redact sensitive fields before a prompt reaches the model, so the work continues and the data doesn’t travel.[Prompt Security](https://www.n-able.com/press/press-releases/as-ai-accelerates-cyberattacks-n-able-and-sentinelone-expand-their-strategic-partnership-to-advance-resilience) , powered by SentinelOne and delivered through N-central, inspects prompts, file uploads, and responses in real time, detecting and redacting data such as PII, PHI, financial information, and source code before it reaches an AI model. Regulated data reaching an unsanctioned AI model can trigger breach-assessment or notification obligations, while limited logging can make the incident difficult to reconstruct.


### **Apply least privilege to AI tools and agents**


Grant AI tools only the access they need for their defined purpose, applying the same principle of least privilege to AI agents that you would apply to users or service accounts. Access controls should reflect what each tool can do. Generative AI that drafts, summarizes, or makes recommendations, with a human reviewing the output before action is taken, generally carries less operational risk than agentic AI that can act directly on systems.


This is where generative and agentic AI security begin to diverge. When a tool moves from recommending an action to taking one, such as triggering automation, modifying workflows, or interacting directly with operational environments, incorrect outputs or unexpected behavior can affect real-world operations. Agentic AI therefore calls for tighter permissions and oversight that reflect the risk of the actions it can take. The shift from[AI that advises to AI that acts](https://www.n-able.com/blog/ai-risk-management-when-ai-moves-from-suggestion-to-action) increases the need for control, particularly when an agent has broad access to sensitive data or critical systems.


### **Vet third-party AI tools and vendors**


Vet any third-party AI tool before you approve it by asking the vendor a short set of direct questions about how they handle your data. Even when a vendor provides the AI system, your organization remains responsible for how that system interacts with your environment and data. Vendor assurances alone aren’t enough protection.


Ask these before approving a tool:


- **Data retention:** What customer data does the system retain, and for how long?
- **Model training:** Is data used to train models, and can that training be disabled?
- **Logging:** What audit logs are available, and can they export to your own logging systems?
- **Tenant separation:** How is data kept separate across customers?
- **Incident response:** Can the feature be limited by role or disabled quickly if problems occur?


If a vendor can’t clearly answer basic questions about data handling, model training, and logging, treat that as a risk signal and reconsider deployment.


### **Monitor AI use and keep evidence**


Monitor AI use continuously and keep a usage record, because an AI policy in a document isn’t proof that governance is working. Ongoing monitoring watches for drift, unexpected behavior, and usage that falls outside approved boundaries. A policy you set and forget can’t catch a vendor model update that changes how a tool behaves or an employee who finds a workaround.


Evidence is what turns governance from aspirational into defensible. Auditors and cyber insurers may ask for evidence of which AI tools are in use and how organizations oversee them. Maintain records detailed enough to understand and investigate AI activity, including relevant timestamps, identities, events, and outcomes. These records can support internal oversight, audits, and compliance efforts. When an auditor or insurer asks for an AI inventory, the goal is to produce one on demand rather than scramble to assemble it.


### **Plan for AI-related incidents and train people**


Build AI into your incident response plan and train people on approved tools and safe data handling, because technology controls work best alongside prepared teams. Define which events trigger investigation: unauthorized AI actions, logging failures, unexpected behavior changes, and vendor model updates that alter how a tool behaves. Treat an AI incident with the same rigor as any other security event.


Training closes the loop. Risky AI use can come from people trying to work faster rather than acting with malicious intent, so clear guidance on approved tools and what data should not be entered into them can help reduce incidents. Coaching at the point of use, including directing someone to an approved alternative rather than simply blocking access, can also reduce the incentive to seek workarounds that move AI usage outside IT’s visibility.


## **AI security checklist**


This AI security checklist summarizes the seven practices for quick reference. Use it as a starting point to assess where your program stands today and what to tackle next.


**Practice**


**What it covers**


See which AI tools are in use Detect shadow AI across endpoints, browsers, extensions, and network traffic before writing any policy


Set an AI acceptable use policy Define approved tools, data rules, ownership, and an approval path in plain language


Protect sensitive data in prompts Inspect and redact PII, source code, and credentials at the point of use


Apply least privilege to AI tools and agents Scale access to purpose; add guardrails and human approval for agentic AI


Vet third-party AI tools and vendors Ask about data retention, model training, logging, and tenant separation before approving


Monitor AI use and keep evidence Watch for drift and log actions in detail for audits and insurer reviews


Plan for incidents and train people Build AI into incident response and coach people on approved tools and data handling


## **How to start applying these practices today**


Start by finding out what AI is already in use, then layer data protection and access controls on top of that visibility. You don’t need a finished program to begin. You need an answer to one question: which AI tools are running in your environment, by whom, and how often. That inventory tells you where the real risk sits and keeps you from drafting policy for tools you can’t see.


Once you have visibility, work through the sequence. Create a short acceptable use policy based on the tools you identify. Add controls to help keep sensitive data out of prompts. Tighten access for AI tools that can take action. Then build the monitoring and evidence needed to make your approach defensible. Teams can use a recognized structure to build a repeatable AI risk management framework, even when certification is not the immediate goal. Treating risk management as an ongoing loop rather than a one-time project can make that approach easier to apply as AI use evolves.


## **Build resilience before the next AI-accelerated threat**


Reactive, alert-driven security can leave teams struggling to keep pace as AI accelerates the threat landscape. Governing AI use is one part of a[broader resilience strategy](https://www.n-able.com/resilience-ai) that has to span before, during, and after an attack.

It breaks down how AI reshapes both the attack surface and the defense model, and how to layer AI approaches to balance speed, accuracy, and trust. ## **Frequently asked questions**


### **What is shadow AI?**


Shadow AI is the unsanctioned use of AI tools across an environment, outside any approval or inventory process. It includes public chatbots, browser extensions, IDE plugins, and API access that employees adopt to work faster, usually without IT’s knowledge. Because these tools can send data to external model providers, shadow AI is where much of an organization’s AI risk concentrates.


### **How is AI security different from traditional cybersecurity?**


AI security differs from traditional cybersecurity because there’s no fixed perimeter to lock down. Traditional security assumes known inputs, approved users, and controlled outputs you can harden at the edge. AI tools accept open-ended natural language, produce probabilistic outputs, and increasingly sit inside browsers and APIs, so the risk lives in the interaction itself rather than at a network boundary. That shifts the point of control to where AI is actually used.


### **Do small IT teams need an AI policy?**


Yes, small IT teams need an AI acceptable use policy, because people are likely already using AI tools whether or not anyone has approved them. A policy doesn’t have to be long. A single page naming approved tools, data rules, and who to ask for exceptions gives a lean team enforceable guidance. Start with visibility into what’s in use, then write the policy against the tools you actually find.


### **What is prompt injection, and why does it matter for LLM security?**


Prompt injection is an attack that hides malicious instructions in text an LLM processes, such as a user prompt, a web page, an email, or a shared document. The model can’t reliably tell trusted instructions from untrusted content, so an attacker can override its guardrails, expose sensitive data, or trigger unwanted actions through connected tools. The risk grows as LLMs gain access to files, browsers, and APIs. Effective LLM security depends on limiting what each AI tool can access, treating external content as untrusted, requiring human approval for high-impact actions, and monitoring how LLMs are used.


### **Is the NIST AI RMF mandatory?**


No, the[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) is voluntary guidance, not a regulatory mandate. That said, it can provide a useful structure for managing AI risk and supporting compliance conversations.
